# Introduction

Player value in basketball is still most often summarised with box-score composite indices that add positive actions and subtract negative ones. In the EuroLeague the official index is the Performance Index Rating (PIR). Such indices are transparent and easy to compute, but their weights lack a formal justification [@carta2026winscore], an index built from the same box-score data was more valid and reliable than PIR [@marmarinos2019structural], and simple efficiency indices measure productivity rather than efficiency and give much weight to scoring [@senatore2022efficiency; @martinez2012factors]. Metrics should therefore be judged by how consistent they are over time and how well they relate to winning [@berri2012measuring], and by their stability, discrimination and independence [@franks2016meta]. Nevertheless, operational-research approaches to team building have turned player evaluations into optimisation problems [@muniz2022sports]; in earlier work on the present data (the author's doctoral thesis), a PIR-type index was maximised with integer linear programming to select lineups. Whether these values capture what matters for winning lineups is less clear. Box-score indices reward rebounds, blocks and high-percentage shots near the basket and do not account for teammates or opponents, whereas regularised adjusted plus-minus (RAPM) estimates each player's contribution to the score while on court, adjusted for the other nine players [@grassetti2020extended; @hvattum2019comprehensive; @terner2021modeling].

Two consequences follow if box-score indices depend on player role over and above on-court impact. First, players with different functions would not be comparable on the same scale; with data-driven roles increasingly used to describe players [@ribes2026identifying; @kalman2020lineup], such a dependence can be measured directly. Second, an optimisation model that maximises the sum of these values would systematically favour some roles and could select lineups that do not perform better on court. Moreover, optimising over noisy estimates tends to select options whose estimated value is inflated, so their realised value is disappointing [@smith2006optimizer]. Lineup choices have been modelled with substitution effects [@gomez2016exploring], substitution networks [@guo2022exploring] and Shapley-value rankings used to form best lineups [@metulini2022measuring], but optimised lineups are rarely compared with what coaches actually do, although the coach's rotation is the natural benchmark that any decision aid must beat; lineup quality can be predicted from individual player data [@martonosi2023predicting], but such predictions are rarely set against coaches' own choices.

The aims of this study were therefore (1) to quantify how strongly PIR-type indices and RAPM depend on player role, including for players with the same RAPM (a proxy for on-court impact); (2) to compare their ability to predict lineup performance out of sample; and (3) to test whether lineups selected by integer programming from these values outperform the players coaches use most. Here we show that box-score indices rate interior roles higher than players with the same impact in other roles whereas RAPM does not, that RAPM predicts future lineup outcomes better, and that optimised lineups show no detectable advantage over the coach's own most-used players.
